An ending is a very small part of a story

When disasterdoesn’t happen.

A safe landing tells you how an account ends. It cannot tell you how the crew got there. Open one real record, then see what happens when thousands of stories become codes.

ACN 2281528September 2025 · 2 narratives

Source: NASA Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS). Original paraphrases of two crew accounts. These are voluntary reports; NASA does not verify them. The controls change what you can read, not what happened.

Counts are database records, not flights or people. Groups can overlap. The 6,127-record cohort covers Full Form records with occurrence months in 2025, retrieved September 29, 2026; it includes unmanned aviation. It is not a census of aviation events.

03 / Read past the label

Recovery is a process.
A code is a handle.

Five deliberately chosen readings test that distinction. Some add context. Others challenge the tempting idea that a recovery code means a clean outcome—or a single agreed story.

The absence of a disaster
is not the absence of a story.

A successful ending can sit beside an unfinished checklist, missing instructions, conflicting recollections or physical damage. Restoring the sequence makes the work of recovery visible. Restoring the voices keeps its uncertainty visible too.

These accounts can help us ask better questions. They cannot tell us how likely a crash was, prove what caused an event, or establish what would have happened if someone had acted differently.

What exactly is being counted?

6,127 Full Form database records. The public ASRS query used occurrence dates 01/2025–12/2025, Full Form selected, Abbreviated unselected, all other filters empty. Full Form was the modern interface’s default; this is an intentional cohort boundary, not all submitted reports. These records contain 7,527 populated narrative slots; 1,298 records have more than one.

The two six-month exports contain 3,086 and 3,041 unique ACNs. Their union exactly matches the year-query ID list. The modern CSV export enforces 5,000 records per download, despite the older introduction’s 10,000 figure. No limit was bypassed.

367 records contain the exact Flight Crew result Executed Go Around / Missed Approach. The 132 combinations are distinct sets across the General, Flight Crew, Air Traffic Control and Aircraft result fields, including blanks. Codes within each field are treated as an unordered set. Multiple codes in one row do not establish time order, a common actor or causation.

Counts of 60, 15 and 105 respectively mean: the same go-around record also contains Requested ATC Assistance / Clarification; Aircraft Damaged; or at least two populated narrative slots. These are overlapping descriptions, not competing outcome categories. “Only the go-around result” means the other three result fields are blank and no additional Flight Crew result is coded (82 records).

How to read the marks, the gaps and the voices

Each mark represents one ACN (ASRS record number). In the open view, four colored bars count codes in four result fields. Their position is a field layout, never a timeline. Similar-looking marks can contain different words: inspect a record for the exact source values. The order is ascending ACN, not event time. Larger selections use smaller marks; the slider and buttons remain available.

Blank means no value is present in the exported field. It does not mean an event or action did not occur. None Reported / Taken is an explicit source category and is kept separate from a blank. “ZZZ” denotes deliberate deidentification in the original; we do not infer missing locations. No distance, altitude or elapsed-time measurements are plotted here.

ASRS can combine several participants’ reports into one record, edit repetitive supplemental narrative and use supplemental details in the primary record. Narrative slots are neither a count of independent events nor proof of independent corroboration. The five readings are original editorial paraphrases; their ordinal steps summarize reported order. The six opening steps are not a flight reconstruction or an operational procedure.

The code archive includes detection values, all four result fields, all anomaly columns, narrative-slot counts and callback presence. It omits reporter prose, synopses, identities, locations, aircraft/person detail and measurements. Unabridged exports and preparation scripts are retained for reproducibility outside the public page.

Source: NASA ASRS Database Online. To read a case, open Report Number (ACN), enter its seven-digit number, then Search. The site does not provide a verified per-record link in this interface; source links here open the search tool with the number shown beside them. The database may evolve after this snapshot.

What this archive cannot answer

ASRS accounts are voluntary and unvalidated. Selection into the reporting system and this public database is not known. These counts cannot estimate national incidence, safety trends, airport or airline performance, or accident probability. Not every record is a near miss; a safe ending does not measure how close an accident was.

Analysts’ categories support retrieval and reading. They are not adjudicated causes or a basis for a causal “human error percentage.” The cases were chosen for explanatory contrast, primarily from an initial September sample; they are not a representative sample of recovery. This is an exploration of evidence and description, not flight instruction.
